I'll work in the category **Set** (the problem refers to "the set T"). The idea: quotient ℝ by the equivalence relation "differ by a multiple of 12"; the set of equivalence classes is naturally represented by [0, 12) via the remainder map.

---

**Construction.** Define two parallel arrows $f, g : \mathbb{R} \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}$ by
$$f(x) = x, \qquad g(x) = x + 12,$$
and define $q : \mathbb{R} \to [0,12)$ by
$$q(x) = x - 12\lfloor x/12 \rfloor \quad (\text{the unique element of } [0,12) \text{ congruent to } x \pmod{12}).$$

We claim $([0,12),\, q)$ is the coequalizer of $f$ and $g$.

---

**Step 1 — $q$ coequalizes $f$ and $g$.** For every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, using $\lfloor (x+12)/12 \rfloor = \lfloor x/12 \rfloor + 1$:
$$q(g(x)) = q(x+12) = (x+12) - 12\bigl(\lfloor x/12\rfloor + 1\bigr) = x - 12\lfloor x/12\rfloor = q(x) = q(f(x)).$$
Hence $q \circ f = q \circ g$.

**Step 2 — $q$ is surjective.** For any $t \in [0,12)$ we have $\lfloor t/12 \rfloor = 0$, so $q(t) = t$. Thus every $t \in [0,12)$ lies in the image of $q$.

**Step 3 — Universal property.** Let $h : \mathbb{R} \to Y$ be any function with $h \circ f = h \circ g$, i.e.
$$h(x) = h(x+12) \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}.$$
By induction this gives $h(x) = h(x + 12k)$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Define $\bar{h} : [0,12) \to Y$ by $\bar{h}(t) = h(t)$ (viewing $t \in [0,12) \subset \mathbb{R}$).

*Factorization:* For every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, write $x = q(x) + 12\lfloor x/12 \rfloor$ with $q(x) \in [0,12)$. Then
$$\bar{h}(q(x)) = h(q(x)) = h\bigl(q(x) + 12\lfloor x/12\rfloor\bigr) = h(x),$$
so $\bar{h} \circ q = h$.

*Uniqueness:* Suppose $\bar{k} : [0,12) \to Y$ also satisfies $\bar{k} \circ q = h$. For any $t \in [0,12)$, take $x = t$ (so $q(t) = t$ by Step 2); then
$$\bar{k}(t) = \bar{k}(q(t)) = h(t) = \bar{h}(t).$$
Hence $\bar{k} = \bar{h}$.

---

**Conclusion.** The map $q : \mathbb{R} \to [0,12)$ satisfies $q \circ f = q \circ g$, and every $h : \mathbb{R} \to Y$ with $h \circ f = h \circ g$ factors uniquely through $q$. Therefore

$$T = [0,12) \;\cong\; \operatorname{Coeq}\bigl(\, \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}},\; (x \mapsto x+12) \,\bigr),$$

with the coequalizer map given explicitly by $q(x) = x \bmod 12$. The equivalence relation induced on $\mathbb{R}$ is $x \sim y \iff x - y \in 12\mathbb{Z}$, and the coset $[x]$ is represented by the unique element $q(x) \in [0,12)$.

I'll work in the category **Set** (the problem refers to "the set T"). The idea: quotient ℝ by the equivalence relation "differ by a multiple of 12"; the set of equivalence classes is naturally represented by [0, 12) via the remainder map.

---

**Construction.** Define two parallel arrows $f, g : \mathbb{R} \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}$ by
$$f(x) = x, \qquad g(x) = x + 12,$$
and define $q : \mathbb{R} \to [0,12)$ by
$$q(x) = x - 12\lfloor x/12 \rfloor \quad (\text{the unique element of } [0,12) \text{ congruent to } x \pmod{12}).$$

We claim $([0,12),\, q)$ is the coequalizer of $f$ and $g$.

---

**Step 1 — $q$ coequalizes $f$ and $g$.** For every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, using $\lfloor (x+12)/12 \rfloor = \lfloor x/12 \rfloor + 1$:
$$q(g(x)) = q(x+12) = (x+12) - 12\bigl(\lfloor x/12\rfloor + 1\bigr) = x - 12\lfloor x/12\rfloor = q(x) = q(f(x)).$$
Hence $q \circ f = q \circ g$.

**Step 2 — $q$ is surjective.** For any $t \in [0,12)$ we have $\lfloor t/12 \rfloor = 0$, so $q(t) = t$. Thus every $t \in [0,12)$ lies in the image of $q$.

**Step 3 — Universal property.** Let $h : \mathbb{R} \to Y$ be any function with $h \circ f = h \circ g$, i.e.
$$h(x) = h(x+12) \quad \text{for all } x \in \mathbb{R}.$$
By induction this gives $h(x) = h(x + 12k)$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

Define $\bar{h} : [0,12) \to Y$ by $\bar{h}(t) = h(t)$ (viewing $t \in [0,12) \subset \mathbb{R}$).

*Factorization:* For every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, write $x = q(x) + 12\lfloor x/12 \rfloor$ with $q(x) \in [0,12)$. Then
$$\bar{h}(q(x)) = h(q(x)) = h\bigl(q(x) + 12\lfloor x/12\rfloor\bigr) = h(x),$$
so $\bar{h} \circ q = h$.

*Uniqueness:* Suppose $\bar{k} : [0,12) \to Y$ also satisfies $\bar{k} \circ q = h$. For any $t \in [0,12)$, take $x = t$ (so $q(t) = t$ by Step 2); then
$$\bar{k}(t) = \bar{k}(q(t)) = h(t) = \bar{h}(t).$$
Hence $\bar{k} = \bar{h}$.

---

**Conclusion.** The map $q : \mathbb{R} \to [0,12)$ satisfies $q \circ f = q \circ g$, and every $h : \mathbb{R} \to Y$ with $h \circ f = h \circ g$ factors uniquely through $q$. Therefore

$$T = [0,12) \;\cong\; \operatorname{Coeq}\bigl(\, \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{R}},\; (x \mapsto x+12) \,\bigr),$$

with the coequalizer map given explicitly by $q(x) = x \bmod 12$. The equivalence relation induced on $\mathbb{R}$ is $x \sim y \iff x - y \in 12\mathbb{Z}$, and the coset $[x]$ is represented by the unique element $q(x) \in [0,12)$.
